questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Assesses ability to choreograph ephemeral canaries using core CKAD primitives: templated Deployment from ConfigMap, secret-based auth, logs via PVC, init containers, probes, and namespace-scoped NetworkPolicy.

## Key Concepts

- ConfigMap templating for Deployment
- Secret-based API tokens and restricted RBAC
- PVC-backed logs and cleanup discipline
- InitContainers for tooling bootstrap
- Readiness/Liveness probes for short-lived canaries
- NetworkPolicy scoped to external dashboard

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: canary-tester
spec:
  schedule: "*/20 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
            - name: install-tools
              image: alpine:3.18
              command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq"]
          containers:
            - name: canary
              image: my-canary-image:latest
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "/canary/run.sh"]
              env:
                - name: DASHBOARD_TOKEN
                  valueFrom:
                    secretKeyRef:
                      name: canary-token
                      key: token
              volumeMounts:
                - name: logs
                  mountPath: /logs
          volumes:
            - name: logs
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: canary-logs
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you rollback a failing canary and propagate the status to the dashboard?
- What are the memory/CPU considerations for rapid-canary spikes and how would you cap them?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
CKAD requires practical mastery of node-scoped components, DaemonSets, hostPath volumes, and real-world log shipping patterns.

## Key Concepts
- DaemonSet on each node with hostPath volumes
- Log tailing with tail -F and sidecar shipping
- ConfigMap-driven batching (BATCH_SIZE)
- NodeSelector to target workers
- Readiness/Liveness probes and lifecycle (preStop)
- Resource requests/limits and rollback strategy

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: log-collector
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-collector
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-collector
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/os: linux
      containers:
      - name: collector
        image: busybox:stable
        command: ["sh","-c","tail -F /var/log/app.log | /usr/local/bin/shipper --endpoint http://log-portal:5000/api/v1/logs --batch-size $(BUS_BATCH)" ]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 15
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 30
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["sh","-c","sleep 10"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        hostPath:
          path: /var/log
          type: Directory
``` 

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test under burst log loads and verify end-to-end delivery? 
- How would you rollback a DaemonSet rollout if a regression is found?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical CKAD debugging: handling slow-start upgrades with probes, init containers for bootstrapping state, and PD&B safeguards to prevent downtime during maintenance.

## Key Concepts

- startupProbe and readinessProbe tuning
- initContainer for pre-warming caches
- PodDisruptionBudget for upgrade safety
- RollingUpdate strategy and rollback procedures

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal patch sketch (Deployment snippet)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: invoice-processor
  namespace: payments
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: init-cache
        image: invoice-processor:2.1
        command: ["sh", "-c", "cp /config/* /var/cache/ || true"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config
          mountPath: /config
        - name: cache
          mountPath: /var/cache
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: invoice-processor:2.1
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
      volumes:
      - name: config
        secret:
          secretName: app-secret
      - name: cache
        emptyDir: {}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you adapt this for a cluster with limited CPU headroom?
- What metrics would you monitor to confirm startup health and cache warmth?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Security hardening of container runtimes and correctness of patching deployments are critical in real-world CKAD tasks.

## Key Concepts
- SecurityContext: runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, readOnlyRootFilesystem, capabilities drop
- Probes: readiness and liveness on /healthz
- Deployment strategy: RollingUpdate for zero-downtime upgrades
- Validation: load testing, rollout status, and rollback workflow

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: portal
  namespace: secure-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0
      maxSurge: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: portal
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: portal
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.25
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 10001
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities:
            drop:
            - ALL
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
          timeoutSeconds: 2
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
          timeoutSeconds: 2
``` 

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adjust if the app requires a limited capability set?
- How would you implement canary rollouts and monitor for regression?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests InitContainer sequencing, one-time data seeding, ConfigMap usage, and ensuring idempotent seeds and probes work with startup order.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainers run before app containers
- Seed data via idempotent SQL (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING)
- Mount seed script from ConfigMap
- Probes and resource requests/limits to keep health
- Validation under load and restart scenarios

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: inventory
  namespace: retail
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: seed-data
        image: postgres:15
        command: ["psql", "-h", "inventory-db", "-U", "seeduser", "-d", "inventory"]
        args: ["-f", "/seed/init.sql"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: seed-scripts
          mountPath: /seed
        env:
        - name: PGPASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: inventory-db-secret
              key: password
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: inventory-app:latest
        env:
        - name: DB_HOST
          value: "inventory-db"
        - name: DB_USER
          value: "seeduser"
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: inventory-db-secret
              key: password
      volumes:
      - name: seed-scripts
        configMap:
          name: inventory-seed-scripts
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests the candidate's ability to compose namespace-scoped config reloads using standard primitives (InitContainers, sidecars, Secrets, PVCs, and NetworkPolicies) without custom operators, focusing on reliability and reload semantics.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer bootstraps config from central API
- Sidecar monitors config changes and signals main app
- Secrets for API tokens and credentials
- Shared volume for config sync
- PVC for logs and /logs
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricts egress to config API

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-reload
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: config
          emptyDir: {}
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: logs-claim
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: your-app:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/app/config
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /var/log/app
        - name: reloader
          image: myorg/config-reloader:latest
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while true; do sleep 300; done"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/app/config
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you validate config before applying a hot reload?
- How would you handle partial reload failures or rollback?

## Why This Is Asked
This question assesses familiarity with ConfigMap mounts, InitContainers, and sidecar reload patterns within a single namespace. It also evaluates understanding of signal-based versus in-process reload mechanisms, along with basic security practices using Secrets and NetworkPolicies.

## Key Concepts
- **ConfigMap-driven runtime config**: Externalizing configuration allows updates without rebuilding containers
- **InitContainer provisioning**: Installing tooling (inotify-tools) needed by sidecars or main containers
- **Sidecar watching**: File change detection using inotifywait triggers graceful reloads without container restart
- **Signal-based reloads**: SIGHUP triggers graceful reloads; alternative approaches include local /reload API endpoints
- **Security with Secrets**: Sensitive data like admin credentials should mount via Secrets, not environment variables
- **NetworkPolicy**: Namespace-level egress restrictions limit exposure of internal endpoints

## Trade-offs
- **Signal vs. API reload**: SIGHUP requires the application to handle signals gracefully; /reload APIs add complexity but offer finer control
- **inotifywait vs. polling**: inotifywait is event-driven and efficient but limited to the container filesystem; polling works cross-platform but incurs overhead
- **Sidecar vs. embedded reload**: Sidecars keep concerns separated but add resource overhead; embedding reload logic reduces complexity but couples concerns
- **ConfigMap vs. volume plugins**: Native ConfigMap mounts require pod recreation for updates; external volume plugins enable dynamic updates at the cost of complexity

## Why This Is Asked

This question tests hands-on CKAD skills: in-cluster configuration, API access, and multi-resource coordination. It evaluates how the candidate wires ConfigMaps, Secrets, and PVCs into a Deployment, and how they enforce traffic restrictions with a NetworkPolicy.

## Key Concepts

- Namespace-scoped Deployment and RBAC permissions
- ConfigMap-based thresholds and Secret-based credentials
- API access to Namespace ResourceQuota metrics
- InitContainer usage for tools like curl/jq
- Logs persisted to a PVC mounted at /logs
- Readiness and liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy to restrict egress to the central endpoint

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: alert-config
data:
  cpu-threshold: "80"
  memory-threshold: "85"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: alert-credentials
data:
  api-key: <base64-encoded-key>
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: log-storage
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: resource-watcher
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: resource-watcher
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: resource-watcher
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: installer
          image: busybox
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |-
                wget -q https://github.com/stedolan/jq/releases/download/jq-1.6/jq-linux64 -O /usr/local/bin/jq
                chmod +x /usr/local/bin/jq
                apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /usr/local/bin
      containers:
        - name: watcher
          image: your-watcher-image:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
              name: http
          env:
            - name: CENTRAL_ENDPOINT
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: alert-credentials
                  key: api-key
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
              readOnly: true
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "64Mi"
              cpu: "50m"
            limits:
              memory: "128Mi"
              cpu: "100m"
      volumes:
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: log-storage
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: alert-config
        - name: tools
          emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-restriction
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: resource-watcher
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              name: central-monitoring
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 443
```

## Trade-offs

1. **Polling vs. Watch API**: Polling ResourceQuota is simpler but adds latency; the Watch API is more efficient but requires handling event streams.
2. **Sidecar vs. Main Container**: A sidecar could handle logging while the main container focuses on monitoring—improving separation of concerns.
3. **Centralized vs. Per-Namespace**: Deploying per-namespace increases resource usage but provides isolation and reduces blast radius.
4. **PVC for Logs**: Using a PVC adds persistence but requires storage provisioning; consider sidecar streaming to stdout for easier management.
5. **InitContainer Overhead**: Downloading tools on every pod start slows startup; a custom image with tools pre-installed would be faster.

## Code Example
```yaml

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: snapshot-app-data
  namespace: <ns>
spec:
  schedule: "0,30 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: init-tools
            image: alpine:3.18
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl kubectl; sleep 0"]
          containers:
          - name: snapshotter
            image: my-snapshot-agent:latest
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: logs-<ns>
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          nodeSelector:
            kubernetes.io/os: linux
```

```yaml

metadata:
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests secret handling, TLS/mTLS basics, mounting certs, and correct network isolation for a real-world integration.

## Key Concepts
- Secrets and volume mounts
- TLS/Certificates and mTLS basics
- NetworkPolicy egress controls
- Rollout and secret rotation strategies

## Code Example
```javascript
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: tls-secret
type: Opaque
data:
  tls.crt: <base64>
  tls.key: <base64>
  ca.crt: <base64>
```

```javascript
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  namespace: prod
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: payments
        image: payments-api:latest
        env:
        - name: TLS_PATH
          value: /certs
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tls
          mountPath: /certs
      volumes:
      - name: tls
        secret:
          secretName: tls-secret
```

```javascript
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: payments-egress
  namespace: prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payments-api
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 203.0.113.45/32
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
```

> Note: DNS-based egress restrictions are not widely supported in NetworkPolicy; use the processor’s IP in the ipBlock.
